Lukewarmness
LOOK-warm-nuhs
noun (spiritual condition)
From lukewarm, Middle English lewk (tepid) + warm; the condition Christ names in the church of Laodicea, "neither cold nor hot" (Rev 3:15).

Biblical Definition

Lukewarmness is the spiritual condition of the church at Laodicea, which the risen Christ rebukes in the last of the seven letters: "I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth" (Rev 3:15-16). It is the temper of self-sufficient complacency. Laodicea was rich, a banking and clothing city famed for a medicinal eye-salve, and the church had taken on the spirit of the town: "I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing" (Rev 3:17). Christ exposes the deadly self-deception — that they were in truth "wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked." To such He gives counsel sharpened to their own trades: "buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed... and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see" (Rev 3:18). Yet even this letter of severest warning carries the tenderest call: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock" (Rev 3:20). The remedy is to "be zealous therefore, and repent" (Rev 3:19). This dictionary confesses that lukewarmness is no harmless middle state but a thing Christ loathes, and that the only cure is the zeal of true repentance and renewed dependence on Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

The complacent, self-sufficient state of the Laodicean church, "neither cold nor hot," which Christ threatens to spue out of His mouth. The remedy is to buy gold tried in the fire and to be zealous and repent.

LUKEWARMNESS, noun. The tepid, self-satisfied spiritual state of the church at Laodicea, neither cold nor hot.

Marked by the boast "I am rich... and have need of nothing," while truly poor and blind.

"So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth" (Rev 3:16).

Christ counsels the lukewarm to buy of Him gold tried in the fire and eyesalve to see.

The remedy: "be zealous therefore, and repent" (Rev 3:19).

Key Scripture

Rev 3:15 — "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot."

Rev 3:16 — "So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth."

Rev 3:17 — "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:"

Rev 3:19 — "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent."

Modern Corruption

Lukewarmness faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the searching Laodicean warning against complacency masking spiritual poverty.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger Christ names at Laodicea is perennial and pressing, perhaps nowhere more than in a comfortable and prosperous age. The lukewarm church is not the persecuted church nor the heretical one; it is the satisfied one, sure of its wealth and unaware of its want. The deadliness lies precisely in the self-deception: "thou knowest not that thou art wretched" (Rev 3:17).

The positive principle to recover is the costly grace Christ offers in answer: gold tried in the fire, white raiment, and eyesalve — true righteousness, true covering, and true sight, all bought of Him and from no other store. The remedy is not redoubled self-effort but renewed dependence, "be zealous therefore, and repent" (Rev 3:19), opening the door to the Christ who knocks (Rev 3:20). This dictionary confesses that the chastening which exposes our poverty is a token of His love, and that the cure for the tepid heart is to come empty to Christ and be made rich in Him.

Hebrew Roots

The word renders the Laodicean condition of tepid water — neither the cold of a refreshing spring nor the heat of a healing bath — fit only to be spued out.

expand to see more

Lukewarm, Middle English lewk, tepid, joined to warm.

Laodicea's water arrived tepid by aqueduct, sickening to drink.

Christ likens the church's state to that nauseating tepidity.

Neither the cold of a spring nor the heat of a bath profits.

The remedy is the zeal and repentance of Revelation 3:19.

Usage

"Lukewarmness is the besetting peril of a prosperous and untroubled church."

"Christ deals more sharply with lukewarmness than with open opposition."

"The cure for lukewarmness is to buy of Christ the gold tried in the fire."
